items.title:
Budget the logs.
Keep the evidence.
items.subtitle: Start with detection needs. Preserve the evidence your obligations require.
items.test: Trace one detection to its source. Explain the cost and the consequence of losing that evidence.
items.boundary: No detection does not mean no value. Audit, investigation and retention duties still apply.
items.alt: SHAMS design loop: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Measure is highlighted and enlarged. Detection-first log budget: name the event and response owner, map the source fields and timing with audit obligations, generate a safe test event to verify detection coverage, then choose the storage tier, retention period and accountable owner. Trace one detection to its source and explain the cost and consequence of losing that evidence. Logs without a detection may still be required for audit, investigation or retention obligations.

items.title: Name the detection
items.detail: Define the event and who will respond.

items.title: Map the required source
items.detail: Specify fields, timing and audit obligations.

items.title: Test the coverage
items.detail: Generate a safe event. Verify the alert.

items.title: Set retention + cost
items.detail: Choose tier, period and accountable owner.

items.title:
Change the assumption.
Trace the consequence.
items.subtitle: A component swap can change the decision underneath it.
items.test: Remove the preferred model. Name the first acceptance test that now needs to run again.
items.boundary: A design exercise, not a claim that any replacement is equivalent.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Measure is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A four-station trace runs down a spine. One: change one assumption, such as the model disappearing, the refresh slowing or a draft step starting to send, while the accepted outcome stays fixed. Two, working backward: find the first dependency that can no longer support that outcome. Three: trace what must change, including permissions, tests, costs and owners. Four: prove it again with a fresh behavioral evaluation, because new authority needs new acceptance evidence, until another engineer can follow it. Evidence in: accepted outcome and changed assumption. Artifact out: affected tests and a decision owner. A replacement is not assumed to be equivalent.

steps.title: Change one assumption
steps.detail: The model disappears. The refresh slows. A draft step starts sending.

steps.title: Find the first break
steps.detail: Which dependency can no longer support the accepted outcome? Start there, not at the new part.

steps.title: Trace what must change
steps.detail: A new part can need new access, a new budget and a new owner.

steps.title: Prove it again
steps.detail: Fresh behavioral evaluation. New authority needs new evidence.

items.title:
Choose the boundary.
Then choose the model.
items.subtitle: Size alone is not a safety control. Route work on task evidence.
items.test: Run the same labeled cases through both routes. Compare accepted results, failures, latency and full cost.
items.boundary: Model suitability depends on the task and evaluation; no savings are assumed.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Measure is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A decision gate asks whether the smaller route passes the same task contract, decided with typed input, expected output, validation and escalation cases. If it passes: use the narrow route, keep validation and permission checks at execution, and confirm answers are correct, supported by the source and stop when they should. If it fails: escalate or stop by trying a suitable stronger route, asking for human review or declining, without improvising authority. One rule holds on both paths: a larger model still needs the same authority boundary. Evidence in: task contract and labeled cases. Artifact out: an evaluated route and a failure path. No savings are assumed.
items.question: Does the smaller route pass the same task contract?

branches.label: PASSES
branches.title: Use the narrow route
branches.detail: Keep validation and permission checks at execution. Record what changed before the savings.

branches.label: FAILS
branches.title: Escalate or stop
branches.detail: Try a suitable stronger route, ask for review, or decline. Do not improvise authority.

items.rule: A larger model still needs the same authority boundary.

items.title:
A handover needs
three reproducible results.
items.subtitle: Give the next operator enough evidence to work without your narration.
items.test: Ask a colleague to run all three cases. Every question they must ask you becomes a gap to close.
items.boundary: Teaching cases support a handover. They are not production certification.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. The handover pack lists the permitted outcome, source versions, tool contracts, stop conditions and a named owner. Three rows follow, each a case, what to inspect and what to keep. Allowed: inspect the intended business state reached by the permitted path, keep inputs and receipt. Refused: inspect that no forbidden change happened and the reason is readable, keep reason and boundary. Recovered: inspect a reconciled final state after the failure, keep steps and timings. Rule: every question they must ask you is a gap to close. Evidence in: allowed, refused and recovery cases. Artifact out: a reproducible operator handover. Teaching cases are not production certification.

rows.subject: Allowed
rows.action: The intended business state, reached by the permitted path

rows.subject: Refused
rows.action: No forbidden change, and a reason the operator can read

rows.subject: Recovered
rows.action: A reconciled final state after the failure

items.rule: Every question they must ask you is a gap to close.

items.title:
Design backward
from the finish line.
items.subtitle: Start with a safely completed task, then trace what must be true.
items.test: Give the acceptance statement to someone else. Can they tell a finished task from a plausible-looking output?
items.boundary: An interface sketch may test a need; it does not prove the engine.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Scope is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A four-station trace runs backward from the finish line. One: the accepted outcome, what must be true for someone to accept the work, for example the right team owns the request. Two, what proves it: the evidence, the record that proves acceptance and who can create it. Three, who may change it: state and authority, the permitted state change and its recovery. Four, what each part must do: the component contract, an input, an output and a test for each capability. A dashed arrow runs the other way to show that building goes forward from the contract. Evidence in: people, need and consequence. Artifact out: an accepted outcome and component contracts. A sketch does not prove the engine.

steps.title: Accepted outcome
steps.detail: What must be true for someone to accept the work?
chips: The right team owns the request

steps.title: Evidence
steps.detail: Which record proves acceptance, and who can create it?

steps.title: State + authority
steps.detail: Which state change is permitted, and how is it recovered?

steps.title: Component contract
steps.detail: Give each capability an input, an output and a test.

items.title:
Give the pilot
an exit decision.
items.subtitle: Agree on the evidence, thresholds and review date before the build.
items.test: Write the decision date, acceptance thresholds and accountable owner before starting the next pilot.
items.boundary: Thresholds depend on the use case. This template supplies no universal target.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Scope is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A decision gate asks: at the review date, did the agreed case pass? It is decided with fixed cases, a quality bar, a cost bar and the review date. Yes: a production decision that approves the next bounded investment, operating owner and release conditions. No: stop or revise, record what failed, and require a new hypothesis and a new decision date for any extension. One rule is written before the build: a useful pilot ends with a decision, including a clear no. Evidence in: business hypothesis and constraints. Artifact out: exit criteria, an owner and a review date. No universal threshold is supplied.
items.question: At the review date: did the agreed case pass?

branches.label: YES
branches.title: Production decision
branches.detail: Approve the next bounded investment, operating owner and release conditions.

branches.label: NO
branches.title: Stop or revise
branches.detail: Record what failed. Any extension needs a new hypothesis and a new decision date.

items.rule: A useful pilot ends with a decision, including a clear no.

items.title:
A fallback needs
a smaller promise.
items.subtitle: When a dependency fails, reduce capability explicitly.
items.test: Remove the retrieval source. Verify that the fallback cannot silently send an unsupported answer as fact.
items.boundary: A fallback must earn its own acceptance evidence. Availability is not permission.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A degraded-mode table with four rows, each a mode, its smaller promise and what to put beside it. Stays available: work the remaining evidence still supports, with an owner and stated limits. Read-only: show what is known and change nothing, with an owner and a recovery condition. Queues: accept the request for later, visibly, with an expiry rule and an owner. Stops: refuse actions that lack evidence or authority, with a reason and a next step. Rule: fallback capability must not exceed the original authority. Evidence in: failed dependency and remaining evidence. Artifact out: a bounded fallback and a stop condition. Availability is not permission.

rows.subject: Stays available
rows.action: Work the remaining evidence still supports

rows.subject: Read-only
rows.action: Show what is known. Change nothing.

rows.subject: Queues
rows.action: Accept the request for later, visibly

rows.subject: Stops
rows.action: Refuse actions that lack evidence or authority

items.rule: Fallback capability must not exceed the original authority.

items.title:
Deletion is a route,
not one button.
items.subtitle: Follow a record through its copies and keep the verification result.
items.test: Delete one synthetic record, then search its identifier across every documented copy and derived view.
items.boundary: Retention duties and backup expiry need an agreed policy; do not promise instant erasure.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Anchor is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A copy map asks where the data travels, who owns each copy, how long it lives and how removal is checked. One record then travels down four stops, each with a removal action and a verification. Source: apply the deletion policy, verify the record is absent or sealed. Index and cache: invalidate every derived copy, then search and read again. Exports: track the owner and retention, confirm the disposition. Backups: apply expiry and a restore rule, verify nothing is reintroduced. Evidence in: data lineage and retention obligations. Artifact out: a deletion route and a verification record. Retention duties and backup expiry need an agreed policy, not a promise of instant erasure.

rows.subject: Backups
rows.action: Apply expiry and a restore rule

items.title:
Before comparing charts,
compare the definitions.
items.subtitle: Two correct queries can answer different business questions.
items.test: Trace one row through both revenue definitions. Identify the exact rule that explains the difference.
items.boundary: Illustrative metric contract. The business owner must approve the actual rules.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Anchor is in focus and opened into the diagram below. The metric contract names a definition, time window, included states, conversion rule and business owner. Four rows follow, each a dimension, what to make explicit and the question to ask. Time: window and time zone, which period? Status: booked or collected, gross or net of refunds, which events count? Currency: conversion rule and date, which rate? Corrections: late adjustments and cancellations, included and when? Rule: reconcile one small synthetic ledger by hand in both views. Evidence in: business question and competing queries. Artifact out: a shared metric definition and owner. The business owner must approve the actual rules.

rows.subject: Status
rows.action: Booked or collected. Gross or net of refunds.

items.rule: Reconcile one small synthetic ledger by hand in both views.

items.title:
A cached answer
can outlive permission.
items.subtitle: Data reuse never replaces a current authorization decision.
items.test: Warm the cache, revoke access, then ask again. The cached path must deny what the source path would deny.
items.boundary: A tenant key alone does not prove row-level or user-level authorization.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Harden is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A decision gate asks whether this caller can read this result right now, decided with the caller, tenant, source permission and policy version. Yes: serve the eligible entry after matching tenant, caller scope and the source or policy version, with scope matched and the entry not expired. No: deny the response, and do not serve the old result, its citations or a revealing summary; invalidate or segregate the entry. One rule holds on every delivery: cache the computation, recheck the permission. Evidence in: caller identity and current access policy. Artifact out: authorized reuse or an explicit denial. A tenant key alone does not prove row-level or user-level authorization.
items.question: Can this caller read this result right now?

branches.label: YES
branches.title: Serve the eligible entry
branches.detail: Match tenant, caller scope and the source or policy version before reuse.

branches.label: NO
branches.title: Deny the response
branches.detail: Do not serve the old result, its citations or a revealing summary.

items.rule: Cache the computation. Recheck the permission.

items.title:
A backup is not
a recovered service.
items.subtitle: Restore the dependencies that make the record usable again.
items.test: Restore a synthetic record. Verify identity, dependencies, owner and acceptance before declaring recovery.
items.boundary: A rehearsal is evidence for the cases exercised. It does not guarantee every recovery.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. Four layers build upward and hold up a dashed crown labeled a usable, recovered service. Layer one at the base: a stored copy, a backup job that reports success and nothing more yet. Layer two: restored dependencies, meaning data, configuration and identities in a known order. Layer three: a named recovery owner who decides, hands off and answers for it. Layer four: an accepted outcome, where the path a person needs works and revoked access stays revoked. Rule: a backup proves a job ran, a rehearsal proves the service returns. Evidence in: backup and dependency inventory. Artifact out: restore evidence and a recovery owner. A rehearsal covers only the cases exercised.

items.title: A stored copy
items.detail: A backup job that reports success. Nothing more yet.

items.title: Restored dependencies
items.detail: Data, configuration and identities, in a known order.

items.title: A named recovery owner
items.detail: Someone decides, hands off and answers for it.

items.title: An accepted outcome
items.detail: The path a person needs works. Revoked stays revoked.

items.rule: A backup proves a job ran. A rehearsal proves the service returns.

items.title:
Version the question
behind the metric.
items.subtitle: A schema can stay unchanged while the meaning changes underneath it.
items.test: Change one business definition in a test copy. Can a consumer detect the version change before comparing periods?
items.boundary: A definition change may require restatement; a new label alone is not reconciliation.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Anchor is in focus and opened into the diagram below. An example shows the same field changing meaning: active customer, has an account, becomes recent paid activity. Four contract rows follow, each with what to pin and a change check. Meaning: the business question it answers, what changed? Population: rows included and excluded, who moved in or out? Period: time and currency rules, is history comparable? Version: owner and effective date, were consumers told? Rule: a type check proves shape, meaning needs its own review. Evidence in: current definition and proposed change. Artifact out: a versioned contract and consumer migration. A definition change may require restatement.
items.rule: A type check proves shape. Meaning needs its own review.

items.title:
Draw the dependencies
into the same room.
items.subtitle: Make hidden ownership and coupling visible before choosing a target design.
items.test: Pick one critical workflow. Trace every data, identity, vendor and operating dependency, then name the owner.
items.boundary: Illustrative map, not an inventory of a real organization.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Scope is in focus and opened into the diagram below. One critical workflow sits in the centre with the question who owns the result. Four dependencies surround it, and every tie to the centre carries a dashed tag asking for an owner. Data: sources, shared stores and retention. Identity: service accounts, scopes and permissions. Vendor: service, agreement and exit path. Operations: deploy, restore and escalation. Margin notes read: an unexplained arrow is a discovery question, and tabletop, remove one, what stops? Evidence in: a critical workflow and known dependencies. Artifact out: a dependency map and accountable owners. The map is illustrative, not an inventory of a real organization.
notes: AN UNEXPLAINED ARROW IS A DISCOVERY QUESTION

nodes.title: Data
nodes.detail: Sources, shared stores and how long each is kept.

nodes.title: Identity
nodes.detail: Service accounts, their scopes and who granted them.

nodes.title: Vendor
nodes.detail: The service, the agreement and the way out.

nodes.title: Operations
nodes.detail: Who deploys, who restores and who is called.

items.title:
The clock starts
before execution.
items.subtitle: Queue time belongs in the promise made to the user.
items.test: Hold a test dependency unavailable, then restore it. Inspect which tasks resume, expire or need a new decision.
items.boundary: A queue absorbs pressure. It does not remove the work or its deadline.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A time bar runs left to right through three phases under one bracket labeled one deadline covers all of it. Arrive: accepted into the queue, assigned identity, deadline, priority and a retry-safe work ID. Wait: owned but not complete, showing the oldest pending request beside throughput and defining when work goes stale, with age, expiry and cancel. Finish: execute, review and confirm, rechecking authority first and recording an accepted or expired outcome. Rule: budget equals intake plus wait plus execution plus review plus confirmation. Evidence in: user deadline and queued work. Artifact out: expiry, escalation and an outcome receipt. A queue does not remove the work or its deadline.
items.span: ONE DEADLINE COVERS ALL OF IT

phases.label: ARRIVE
phases.title: Accepted into the queue
phases.detail: Assign identity, deadline, priority and a retry-safe work ID.

phases.label: WAIT
phases.title: Owned, not complete
phases.detail: Show the oldest pending request beside throughput. Define when work goes stale.

phases.label: FINISH
phases.title: Execute, review, confirm
phases.detail: Recheck authority first. Record an accepted or expired outcome.

items.rule: BUDGET = INTAKE + WAIT + EXECUTION + REVIEW + CONFIRMATION

items.title:
Buy the capability.
Test the exit.
items.subtitle: A purchasing decision also chooses the cost of changing your mind.
items.test: Export a synthetic case set and run it through a replacement path. List every field, rule or behavior that was lost.
items.boundary: An export button is not proof of operational portability.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Scope is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A decision gate asks whether another provider can reproduce the required outcome, decided with data export, identity mapping, API limits and acceptance cases. Rehearsed: commit with a known exit, keeping the export format, the acceptance cases and a realistic replacement path. Unproven, shown in gold because it is a cost: price the lock-in first by naming the provider-specific behavior, missing fields and migration work before committing. One rule holds either way: portability is an exercised path, not a feature label. Evidence in: required outcome and supplier constraints. Artifact out: a build-or-buy decision and a tested exit. An export button is not proof.
items.question: Can another provider reproduce the required outcome?

branches.label: REHEARSED
branches.title: Commit with a known exit
branches.detail: Keep the export format, the acceptance cases and a realistic replacement path.

branches.label: UNPROVEN
branches.title: Price the lock-in first
branches.detail: Name the provider-specific behavior, missing fields and migration work before committing.

items.rule: Portability is an exercised path, not a feature label.

items.title:
Keep the decision
inspectable.
items.subtitle: Record what the system received and did. An explanation is not proof.
items.test: Replay one synthetic case from its recorded inputs and versions. Compare the observed actions and result.
items.boundary: A trace supports investigation; it cannot prove a model’s hidden internal reasoning.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A four-station evidence trail runs down a spine. One: request and context, the request and its version with approved source references. Two, checked against: permission decisions, what was allowed, what was refused and under which policy. Three, which produced: actions and outcomes, the tool inputs, results, state changes and cost. Four, kept as: a record for review that captures only what an investigation needs, with redaction, access and retention rules. Evidence in: context, policy and observable actions. Artifact out: an access-controlled investigation trail. A trace cannot prove a model’s hidden internal reasoning.

steps.title: Request + context
steps.detail: The request and its version, with approved source references.

steps.title: Permission decisions
steps.detail: What was allowed, what was refused, under which policy.

steps.title: Actions + outcomes
steps.detail: Tool inputs, results, state changes and cost.

steps.title: A record for review
steps.detail: Capture only what an investigation needs.

items.title:
A rollback cannot
unsend an email.
items.subtitle: Separate reversible system state from effects outside your boundary.
items.test: In a synthetic run, fail after the external effect. Verify the recovery path does not create the effect twice.
items.boundary: A compensating action is a new business action and may need fresh authority.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A time bar runs left to right through three phases under a bracket labeled one workflow, two kinds of undo. A dashed coral marker after the first phase reads external effect sent, and everything after it is drawn in coral. Before: prevent the unnecessary effect by drafting, validating and obtaining the required authorization, while it can still be reversed. After: establish what happened by inspecting the destination receipt before any retry. Recover: choose the right repair, reconcile local state and compensate external effects on purpose, or acknowledge them. Rule: restore code does not equal reverse every business effect. Evidence in: failure point and destination receipt. Artifact out: reconciliation or an authorized repair.
items.span: ONE WORKFLOW, TWO KINDS OF UNDO

phases.label: BEFORE
phases.title: Prevent the unnecessary effect
phases.detail: Draft, validate and obtain the required authorization.

phases.label: AFTER
phases.title: Establish what happened
phases.detail: Inspect the destination receipt before any retry.

phases.label: RECOVER
phases.title: Choose the right repair
phases.detail: Reconcile local state. Compensate or acknowledge external effects.

items.rule: RESTORE CODE ≠ REVERSE EVERY BUSINESS EFFECT

items.title:
Make the foundation
easy to operate.
items.subtitle: Predictable systems leave room for ambitious products.
items.test: Ask a new engineer to trace one release and one restore. Record every undocumented step they need help with.
items.boundary: Prefer simplicity where it fits. A measured requirement can justify an exception.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. Four foundation layers build upward and hold up a dashed crown labeled attention for the product. Layer one at the base: a foundation with headroom, slightly heavier than today needs. Layer two: managed before self-hosted, unless there is a measured reason. Layer three: one deployment path, used by everyone for everything. Layer four: a written owner for every layer. Rule: if a new engineer cannot learn it in an afternoon, it is too interesting. Evidence in: platform responsibilities and dependencies. Artifact out: a repeatable release and a recovery path. A measured requirement can justify an exception.

items.title: A foundation with headroom
Managed before self-hosted
items.detail: Unless there is a measured reason.

items.title: One deployment path
A written owner

items.rule: If a new engineer cannot learn it in an afternoon, it is too interesting.

items.title:
Route by evidence,
not model prestige.
items.subtitle: A cheaper call is useful only if the accepted task stays cheaper.
items.test: Run the same cases through both routes. Include retries, escalation and human correction in the cost.
items.boundary: This is a comparison method, not a claim about a particular model or saving.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Measure is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A decision gate asks whether the cheaper route still passes the acceptance cases, decided with awkward inputs, missing evidence and cases that should escalate. Passes: count the full cost, including validation, retries, failed attempts and human corrections, recorded as cost per accepted task and elapsed time. Fails: escalate by the agreed rule, which is decided before comparing cost, and keep the failed case. The number that matters sits under both paths in gold: cost per accepted task equals total delivery cost divided by accepted work. Evidence in: shared cases and an acceptance rule. Artifact out: route evidence and full delivery cost. No model-specific saving is claimed.
items.question: Does the cheaper route still pass the acceptance cases?

branches.label: PASSES
branches.title: Count the full cost
branches.detail: Include validation, retries, failed attempts and human corrections.

branches.label: FAILS
branches.title: Escalate by the agreed rule
branches.detail: Decide the escalation rule before comparing cost. Keep the failed case.

items.rule: Cost per accepted task = total delivery cost / accepted work

items.title:
Uncertainty needs
an action policy.
items.subtitle: Make the next step depend on evidence and authority, not confidence alone.
items.test: Run synthetic cases for missing context, conflicting sources, denied access and a permitted action. Inspect each.
items.boundary: Model confidence is not a substitute for evidence or authorization.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Harden is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A decision table with four rows, each a condition, the next action and what to verify. Missing context: ask one specific question, verify no invented detail. Sources conflict: hand both sources to the accountable owner, verify both sources were kept. Access denied: do not proceed and decline that request, verify no restricted content was returned. Action permitted: validate, then execute, verify scope and a result receipt. Rule: confidence is one signal, it cannot grant authority. Evidence in: available evidence and caller authority. Artifact out: ask, escalate, refuse or execute. Model confidence is not a substitute for evidence or authorization.

rows.subject: Sources conflict
rows.action: Hand both sources to the accountable owner

rows.subject: Access denied
rows.action: Do not proceed. Decline that request.

items.rule: Confidence is one signal. It cannot grant authority.

items.title:
Keep the rules
with the work.
items.subtitle: Three durable habits, and the check that makes them repeatable.
items.test: Pick one workflow. Locate the written rule, the human decision and the test that proves its foundation.
items.boundary: A reusable checklist helps prepare evidence; it does not certify a system.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A four-station trace runs down a spine. One: write the rule down and give it an owner, an example and an exception path. Two, who may act on it: keep authority explicit, because a human in the loop needs a named action, evidence and time, and mark what the system may prepare, what it may execute and where a person decides. Three, what it stands on: foundation before feature, meaning data, state, permissions, contracts and recovery come first. Four, can it be repeated: hand it to someone else and ask whether they can find a permitted outcome, a refusal and a recovery; keep what they can verify. Evidence in: written rules and human decisions. Artifact out: reusable checks and acceptance evidence. A checklist does not certify a system.

steps.title: Write the rule down
steps.detail: Give it an owner, an example and an exception path.

steps.title: Keep authority explicit
steps.detail: A human in the loop needs a named action, evidence and time.

steps.title: Foundation before feature
steps.detail: Data, state, permissions, contracts and recovery come first.

steps.title: Hand it to someone else
steps.detail: Can they find a permitted outcome, a refusal and a recovery?

items.title:
A small release needs
a small blast radius.
items.subtitle: Limit the consequence, not just the number of changed lines.
items.test: Revoke the release flag during a test run. Check which in-flight actions stop and which need reconciliation.
items.boundary: A flag can stop new work. It cannot automatically undo completed effects.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Sustain is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A decision gate asks whether we can stop this change without guessing who it reached, decided with tenants, records, operations and dependencies. Bounded: expose a named cohort, and name the stop signals, who can halt it and what happens to work in flight. Unbounded: shrink it before rollout by reducing the reach and exercising the stop and reconciliation paths first. One rule applies when the signal fires: observe, stop new work, then reconcile work already done. Evidence in: release scope and permitted effects. Artifact out: a stop signal and a reconciliation plan. A flag can stop new work but cannot undo completed effects.
items.question: Can we stop this change without guessing who it reached?

branches.label: BOUNDED
branches.title: Expose a named cohort
branches.detail: Name the stop signals, who can halt it and what happens to work in flight.

branches.label: UNBOUNDED
branches.title: Shrink it before rollout
branches.detail: Reduce the reach. Exercise the stop and reconciliation paths first.

items.rule: Observe, stop new work, then reconcile work already done.

items.title:
Turn the invoice
into an ownership map.
items.subtitle: Each recurring cost should connect to a workload and a decision.

process.leave_with: Cost ownership + keep or retire decision

items.test: Choose one unexplained charge. Trace its workload, owner, purpose and safe retirement evidence before acting.
items.boundary: A high cost may be justified. Investigate before removing a dependency.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Measure is in focus and opened into the diagram below. Annotate every line with what it is, who owns it and whether anyone would notice if it stopped. Four rows follow, each a bill line, what to connect it to and the decision. Compute: workload and tier owner, look for a tier bought mid-incident, then keep, tune or retire. Storage: data and retention owner, look for growth nobody planned, then need, growth and expiry. Network: flow and service owner, look for a region nobody chose, then purpose and destination. Shared service: consumers and cost owner, look for retired but still running, then allocation and lifecycle. Rule, in gold because the subject is cost: a line with no name beside it is a decision nobody is making. Evidence in: charges and a workload inventory. Artifact out: cost ownership and a keep or retire decision. A high cost may be justified, so investigate before removing a dependency.

items.title:
Reuse the component.
Recheck the decision.
items.subtitle: Keep the knowledge that makes a useful part safe to use again.
items.test: Move the component into a synthetic second context. Change its authority. The old permission must not follow.
items.boundary: Code can be reused. Another organization’s authority cannot be inherited.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Harden is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A four-station trace runs down a spine and describes the package kept beside the code. One: the contract, meaning inputs, outputs and permitted effects. Two, because: the decision record, with the reason, the assumptions about identity, freshness and delivery, and what would change the design. Three, proven by: failure tests, where allowed, refused and recovery cases travel with the part. Four, rechecked in: the new context, where every assumption is tested again for identity, data policy and acceptance, because approval does not travel. Evidence in: component contract and new context. Artifact out: revalidated authority and failure tests. Another organization’s authority cannot be inherited.

items.title:
I approved $500.
Who approved $5,000?
items.subtitle: An approval belongs to the proposal that was actually reviewed.
items.test: Approve version 1, change the amount, then attempt the write. Expected: PAYLOAD_CHANGED; synthetic writes: 0.
items.boundary: Deterministic teaching simulation. No payment, model or cloud transaction is executed.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Harden is in focus and opened into the diagram below. A synthetic teaching example shows two documents. Version 1, reviewed, is a proposal for $500 that a person read. An arrow labeled amount edited leads to version 2, changed, the same request for $5,000. A round approval seal with a person in it is stamped on version 1 only. A dashed coral line from the seal toward version 2 is blocked and labeled approval does not transfer. Version 2 leads down to a coral stop: version 2 needs a new review, PAYLOAD_CHANGED, synthetic writes zero. Evidence in: the exact proposal and a human approval. Artifact out: a version-bound action and a refusal receipt. No payment, model or cloud transaction is executed.

stop.title: Stop: version 2 needs a new review.

items.title:
Budget the logs.
Keep the evidence.
items.subtitle: A log source earns its place by what it lets you detect, explain or prove.
items.test: Trace one detection to its source. Explain the cost and the consequence of losing that evidence.
items.boundary: Logs may also be required for audit, investigation and retention obligations. No current detection is not permission to delete them.
items.alt: SHAMS method map: Scope, Harden, Anchor, Measure, Sustain. Measure is in focus and opened into the diagram below. One log source is asked how it earns its place, and two lanes leave it. Solid lane, a detection uses it: name the detection (the event and a named responder), map the evidence (source, fields and time window), then test the coverage with a controlled event that is detected, investigated and traced back. Example: a privileged role activation joined to identity. Dashed lane, no detection uses it: it may still be owed for audit, investigation or a retention duty, so that is not permission to delete. Both lanes meet in one gold decision: set retention, cost and owner, with the coverage test beside the cost estimate. Evidence in: detection needs and required evidence. Artifact out: a coverage test and a cost owner.
